title: The Hillbilly Attack
description: Although silly in name, this opening has been played by none other than Magnus Carlsen. It's a creative attacking weapon against the Caro-Kann defense. Due to the length of variations, I recommend this above intermediate level.

r2q1r2/pp1b1p1p/2p1k1p1/3p4/3P2PQ/2N4P/P.text:
Black has to capture here.

Now try to think of a checkmate in two moves.

We will use a bit of geometry here and check from e1.

Black has to move the king.

r2q1r2/pp1b1p1p/2p2kp1/3p2N1/3P2PQ/2N4P/.text:
That's why they have to take with the king. Now that king is in the line of attack.

What's the best square to place the knight with a discovered check?

It's actually e6!

We sacrifice the knight in order to cover the g7-square and prevent the king from getting back to safety.

r2q1r2/pp1b1p1p/2p2kp1/3pQ3/3P2P1/2N4P/P.text:
It's checkmate on the next move.

Good game.

r2q1r2/pp1b1pkp/2p2np1/3p2N1/3P2PQ/2N4P/.text:
The only piece preventing us from taking that h7-pawn is the knight on f6.

So we will sacrifice the rook for the knight!

This is a classic tactic to remove a defender.

If Black captures with the queen here, Qxh7# is checkmate.

r2q1rk1/pp1b1pbp/2p2npB/3p2N1/3P2PQ/2N4P.text:
Black has to move the bishop if they don't want to lose it.

And now try to visualize how we want to attack.

First, we need our queen to see the h7-square.

That's why we will trade the bishops.

r2q1rk1/pp1npp1p/2p2npb/5b2/3P3Q/1BN2N2/.text:
You might face Black capturing here, although a lot of players feel uncomfortable with our queen coming to h6.

And that's where our queen will arrive.

It might become dangerous for Black to leave it there for a long time.

r2q1rk1/pp1npp1p/2p3pQ/5b2/3P2n1/1BN2N2/.text:
That's why you might face ...Ng4 often here, attacking the queen.

We shouldn't stay on the h-file anymore.

The d2-square is safest keeping the queen somewhat active.

And as you will see, Black won't be able to hold the h6-square for long.

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/5b2/3P3Q/1BN2N2/.text:
But where should we activate it to, once Black develops the knight to d7?

Well, when a bishop is on g7, it serves as an extremely strong defender of the king.

Our queen is already on h4 and if we want to threaten that king at some point, trading that defender off is a great idea!

r2q1rk1/pp2pp1p/1np2npQ/5b2/3P4/1BN2N1P/.text:
Slide right back to h6!

From there, we can build for g4 to expand.

Our knight can jump to g5 to threaten the h7-pawn together with the queen and there might be some sacrifices lurking on f6, similar to what we've already seen.

The a-rook can join the attack on the e-file.

r2q1rk1/pp2pp1p/1np3p1/5b2/3P2n1/1BN2N2/.text:
While they improve, our plan is...

To attack the knight on g4...

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/1np2npB/5b2/3P3Q/1BN2N2/.text:
Black is rotating the knight to the center via the b6-square.

Our plan of action after h3 is to push g4 at some point, and get our knight to g5 to threaten that h7-pawn.

You will see how basically all of our pieces participate in this beautiful attack.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2npB/3n1b2/3P3Q/1BN2N1.text:
Black centralizes the knight and offers a trade.

That knight is protecting the knight on f6 which we want to remove, as it is the only defender of the h7-pawn.

First, we'll jump to g5. Our plan is as already described.

r2q1rk1/pp3pbp/2p1pnpB/3n1bN1/3P3Q/1BN4P.text:
Black solidifes the knight in the center, but it won't help their cause.

We'll trade in the center now.

r2q1rk1/pp3pbp/2p2npB/3p1bN1/3P3Q/2N4P/P.text:
It makes little sense for Black to recapture with the knight, so they take with the pawn.

Now comes a killer combination.

We can unleash g4!

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/5b2/7Q/1BN2N2/PP.text:
Black does the same.

Now we can begin to think about expanding in the center.

And d4 is definitely the way to go.

We grab space in the center, take more control of the e5-square and are ready to develop our bishop.

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/2p2np1/8/4P2Q/1BN1BP2/P.text:
And I suggest we develop the bishop behind the pawn.

We'll castle queenside next to have a dangerous rook on the d-file.

Almost all of our pieces are on the optimal squares and active.

White is much better.

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/2p2np1/8/4P2Q/1BN2P2/PP.text: Black decides to retreat to d7.

rn1qk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/5b2/7Q/1BN1PP2/PP.text:
And there isn't much Black can do to stop it.

Let's advance the pawn and attack the bishop.

Now we've got a lot of space in the center and we can get the bishop out next.

rn1qk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/5b2/7Q/1BN2N2/PPP.text:
Black gets the bishop out.

We'll castle first.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/5b2/4p2Q/1BN5/PP.text:
Study 1 will deal with 6...Bf5. It's the most popular move played in this position, and you will face it more than half the time.

I suggest we play f3 and offer a trade of pawns, playing in gambit style.

Black capturing will help our development and we would be ready to castle.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/5b2/7Q/1BN1pP2/P.text:
Black can try to disrupt our ideas and push here.

This is a mistake. Black shouldn't give away the pawn like this.

We'll simply take the pawn, since Black offered it this way.

This doesn't hurt our position at all since we are threatening to play e4 now.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/5b2/7Q/1BN2p2/PP.text:
Black capturing on f3 is by far the most common move.

It's easier for players to relieve the tension than complicate things in the center.

We'll recapture with the knight, of course.

Since the pawns have been traded, we have space to push d4 at some point and develop the c1-bishop.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/4qb2/7Q/1BN2R2/PPP.text:
Black activates the bishop...

But we have time to strike in the center, attacking the queen again.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/2pq1np1/5b2/3P1B1Q/1BN2R2.text:
Our last few moves gave a lot of life to our position as we managed to develop and expand with tempo.

White is actually better now, with potential to either improve the bishop to e5 or trade it on h6 at some point and try to attack.

Since we've got the open f-file, doubling the rooks there is the way to go.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/2pq1np1/5b2/3P3Q/1BN2R2/P.text: Once it retreats, we can keep targeting it.

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/4qb2/4p2Q/1BN2P2/.text:
Black retreats to e5.

There is actually no danger here as long as we protect the f3-pawn.

I don't recommend capturing in the center now as we are already down a pawn and don't want many trades to happen.

So we will just castle.

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/4qb2/7Q/1BN2p2/PP.text:
And once Black takes on f3...

We'll recapture with the rook.

Now that the e4-pawn is out of the way, we have a lot of breathing room in the center.

You should always think about this when a central pawn is removed.

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/5b2/3qp2Q/1BN2P2/.text:
A move that protects the e4-pawn instead of capturing is ...Qd4.

Black wants to centralize the queen and keep it active.

However, they can easily get tangled up if they play like this.

Especially if we can develop with a tempo on that queen immediately.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/8/4p2Q/1B6/PPPP1.text:
This will probably force Black to activate the knight and protect the e4-pawn.

And we'll continue attacking the pawn while developing another piece.

We already forced Black to make some moves that might divert them from their usual plan.

Now our play is logical and positional.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with the Caro as they want to place a protected pawn in the center without blocking their light-squared bishop.

And now 2.Bc4 is the Hillbilly attack.

One of the main ideas is to develop the light-squared bishop early and control the center.

This can lead to early attacks as we are also planning to get the queen out soon!

rnbqkbnr/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/7Q/4p3/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
Chapter 1 will deal with Black blocking this attack with ...g6.

It is played almost 50% of the time, in almost 90,000 games. Black will often follow it up with ...Bg7 at some point.

The best square to retreat to is h4. 

The queen plays another role here; attacking the e4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2B1P3/8/PPPP1PP.text:
Black will most likely play ...d5.

And our last move does look odd because our bishop is under attack.

But our point is to retreat and sacrifice the pawn on e4!

We want our bishop to be strong and target the f7-pawn, so that we can threaten a deadly check as early as move 4.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4p3/1B6/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black captures.

And now we'll activate the queen, as mentioned.

We've already got two active pieces out in the opening, eyeing the king.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to our course on the Hillbilly attack.

It's a strong weapon against the Caro-Kann that can throw many players off balance if they don't know the theory.

It is unorthodox and unexpected, which is what makes it useful in many cases.

r1b2r2/pp3pk1/4pqp1/3p2QP/3P4/1B6/PPP4P/.text: And if Black accepts this sacrifice...

r1b2r2/pp3pk1/4pqpP/3p2Q1/3P4/1B6/PPP4P/.text:
We've got the killer move h6+.

The Black king has to move away from the queen in any case.

We will capture it on the next move with a completely winning position.

r1bq1r2/pp2ppk1/6p1/3p2pP/3P3Q/1B6/PPP4P.text:
The reason is...

That we get our queen to the g5-square and pin the g6-pawn.

Now that pawn is weak.

r1bq1r2/pp2ppk1/6pp/3p2Nn/3P2PQ/1B6/PPP4.text:
Instead of jumping back to f6, Black can try to counter attack our knight with ...h6.

But this doesn't work either.

We'll accept this kind of trade.

r1bq1r2/pp2ppkp/2p3p1/3n2Nn/3P3Q/1BN5/PP.text:
The king recaptures.

We'll remove another important piece from the center.

r1bq1r2/pp2ppkp/5np1/3p2N1/3P2PQ/1B6/PPP.text:
Black can try to move back to f6.

But you know the drill already.

r1bq1r2/pp2ppkp/6p1/3p2Nn/3P3Q/1B6/PPP3P.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn again.

And finally, we can play g4.

r1bq1r2/pp3pk1/4p1p1/3p2QP/3P4/1B6/PPP4P.text:
Plus, we've got an amazing tactic if Black plays ...e6 and offers a trade of queens.

Think of a way to block the queens' vision. It's Rf6!

Completely sacrificing the rook, we block Black's queen and target the weakest points in their position.

We are even threatening to double the rooks on the f-file.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pbp/2p1pnp1/6B1/3P3Q/1BN2N.text:
The approach you can implement here is Bg5, pinning the knight on f6.

It's not as easy for Black to untangle from this, so it's a great move.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pbp/2p1pnp1/8/3P3Q/1BN2N2/.text:
Black playing solidly with ...e6 might seem like the way to go, but it only helps our potential attack.

Their light-squared bishop is completely blocked in.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/8/4P2Q/1BN2P2/P.text:
Black continues development themselves.

They are planning ...Nc5 to go after our bishop.

And we'll develop to h3, since we can't to f3.

I prefer this square to the e2-square because we keep options of Ng5 alive.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/8/4P2Q/1BN5/PPP.text:
The knight develops to d7 now, with the already standard idea of ...Nc5.

And we'll get the knight out.

Let Black spend three moves just to trade one piece off.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/8/7Q/1BN2N2/PPP.text:
Expect to see this developing move at some point.

The knight is coming to either b6 or c5.

Our central move prevents one of those squares.

We are ready to place the bishop on h6 now.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/1np2np1/8/3P3Q/1BN2N2/P.text:
Black places the knight on b6.

This is one way to try and defend, bringing the b-knight to the center to support the other knight.

It should not alter our plans of trading off the g7-bishop, though.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/2n5/4P2Q/1BN2N2/.text:
They can do that all day long.

Meanwhile, we'll expand in the center!

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/2n5/4P2Q/1BN2P1N.text:
Black continues with their plan.

Not much we can do about the bishop but develop behind our pawn chain.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/3PP2Q/1nN2N2/P.text:
Black takes.

And we will recapture with the a-pawn, as always.

We've got two healthy pawns in the center now and more space than Black.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/4P2Q/1PN1BP1N/.text:
We'll take back with the a-pawn and preserve that beautiful pawn chain on the light squares, which serves as a replacement for our bishop.

It's not going to be as easy to attack from this spot, but White is positionally doing well either way.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2npB/3n4/3P3Q/1BN2N2/.text:
Black does as intended, centralizing one of the knights.

We should still prepare to attack the king, with the move Ng5.

We've seen this many times. We want to trade the dark-squared bishops at some point and remove the defender from f6 to win the h7-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p3pB/3n2Nn/3P3Q/1BN5/P.text:
Black can actually try to jump to h5 here.

This is another defensive measure you might face.

But we've got g4 to kick that knight away.

First, we'll make a couple of necessary trades.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/7Q/1PN2N2/1PPP2.text: And after Black activates the bishop...

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/7Q/1PNP1N2/1PP3.text:
That plan is to trade off those dark-squared bishops and look to play Ng5!

This is almost always a good idea in the Hillbilly, and that's why f3 is recommended on move 7.

After all this, we want to have an open f-file for the rook which could lead to sacrifices.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npp1p/2p2np1/8/4p2Q/1BN5/PPP.text:
The move 6...Nbd7 is only played 2% of the time, and it definitely seems unnatural.

Instead of doing something about the central pawn, Black develops and blocks their bishop.

We won't even capture in the center.

Let's play the by now traditional f3 idea so that we can get our knight out next.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npp1p/2p2np1/8/7Q/1BN2p2/PPP.text:
Black captures.

We'll take back with the knight.

Now we are ready to castle and already have a big lead in activity.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/2n5/7Q/1BN2N2/PP.text:
That's why you should expect Black to go after your bishop at some point.

This is often the idea behind the early ...Nbd7.

Let's castle here.

There isn't much we can do about the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/8/7Q/1nN2N2/PPPP.text:
Black takes.

And we'll recapture with an open file.

Our plan shouldn't really differ from the usual ideas.

r2q1r2/pp2pp1Q/5kp1/3p2N1/3P2b1/1B6/PPP4.text:
And they do.

How to continue now?

Well, I suggest we slide back to h4.

r2q1r2/pp2pp1p/5kp1/3p2N1/3P2bQ/1B6/PPP4.text:
We already know that the king has to capture.

We don't have to move our knight right away.

First, we can cover the e6-square and prepare Ne6+.

Black doesn't have many options here.

r2q1r2/pp2ppk1/6p1/3p2N1/3P2Q1/1B6/PPP4P.text:
We can actually just capture on g4.

Not all attacks have to end in checkmate.

Now we've got two pieces for the rook and the attack rages on.

White is completely winning.

r2q1r2/pp2ppk1/6p1/3p2N1/3P2bQ/1B6/PPP4P.text:
Black would love a repetition, sure.

But we don't have to give it to them.

r2q1r2/pp2ppkp/5np1/3p2N1/3P2bQ/1B6/PPP4.text:
And that deadly blow...

Is sacrificing the rook on f6, once again.

r2q1r2/pp2ppkp/6p1/3p2N1/3P2bQ/1B6/PPP4P.text:
They can try to return to g7.

But will have to step right back once we capture on h7.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/4N3/3PP1bQ/1PN5/1.text:
But I suggest we jump to e5!

Black doesn't have time to take on d4 because their bishop on g4 is hanging.

They will have to move the bishop first, after which we will activate the bishop and protect d4, keeping our knight active on e5.

Castling is coming too and White is doing great.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/3PP1bQ/1PN2N2/1.text: Sure, they can attack the defender of our d4-pawn.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2npB/3n1bN1/3P3Q/1BN5/.text:
Black actually has a way to try and prolong the defense by blocking the f-file.

But this doesn't work either. There's no escape.

We've got the simple g4! We have to open up the f-file at any cost.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2npB/3n2N1/3P2bQ/1BN5/.text:
The bishop has to either capture or g4 or move away.

First, we'll trade in the center, eliminating the knight defending its partner on f6.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/5npB/3p2N1/3P2bQ/1B6/PPP.text:
Once the pawn recaptures...

We'll trade the bishops too.

This is a standard pair of trades we make before delivering the deadly blow.

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/5b2/1q2p2Q/1BNP1N.text:
That's why sliding to b4 seems logical, as it keeps the queen's sight of the pawn.

It doesn't help Black's cause, however.

Let's take once.

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/5b2/3qp2Q/1BNP4/P.text:
But they can try to protect the pawn.

This only makes matters worse for them, as now they are completely lost!

The way to win is to get the knight out to f3.

If they move the queen away from the e4-pawn, we will simply capture on e4 and have a crushing position.

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/5b2/1q2n2Q/1BN2N2/.text: The knight recaptures, and we can actually play a slower game here.

I suggest we castle.

The knight is pinned to the queen and isn't going anywhere.

Meanwhile, we'll dislodge the queen with a3 soon and Black won't be able to save all pieces.

White is winning.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/8/3qp2Q/1BN5/PPP.text:
A move that's played only 5% of the time but certainly looks dangerous is ...Qd4.

Black centralizes their queen early and protects the pawn.

However, the clear downside is that the e4-pawn is now pinned to the queen.

And we will attack it. Black can't capture on d3.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/4p2Q/1BN2P2/PP.text:
Black can choose to completely ignore our moves and castle.

At this point, we are going to capture. If Black doesn't want to confront us, we'll confront them.

Now we've got extra central space and room to activate our knight to f3.

Also, the d-pawn is coming to d4!

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/7Q/1BN1PP2/PPP.text:
Once Black castles, our plan is actually simple.

First, we'll play e4 since we've been given the space.

We also saw this in the 6...Bf5 study.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/7Q/1BN2N2/PPPP.text:
Black castles.

And we will do the same. The f-file is already open for our rook.

The life our position has lies in the opportunity to expand with d4.

After that, we can look to trade dark-squared bishops and organize an attack.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/4p2Q/1BN5/PPPP1.text:
The most common out of these options is 6...Bg7, and it's played 36% of the time.

Black simply wants to develop quickly and castle, thinking we'll simply capture the pawn in the center.

But it's not that easy. We want rapid development and the f-file for the rook once we castle, so we propose to play gambit style with f3.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/7Q/1BN1pP2/PPPP.text:
Black can try to push ...e3 here.

It does leave our pawn on f3 in a weird spot and block some of our development.

But we have a way around that too.

We'll take the pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/7Q/1BN2p2/PPPP2.text:
Black capturing on f3 is the move you will see the most.

Black wants to keep their extra pawn without worrying.

We'll take back with the knight.

It might seem like we have no compensation for the pawn, but there is actually a lot of potential in our position.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/8/4p2Q/1B6/PPPP1.text:
The most natural defense...

And the most natural attack!

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The Caro-Kann.

We play the Hillbilly.

Our bishop comes out.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/7Q/4p3/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
One of the best moves is to block with the g-pawn.

We'll slide to h4 and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2B1P3/8/PPPP1PP.text:
Black advances in the center and attacks it.

But we'll simply retreat and gambit the pawn on e4.

Our bishop's activity is more important to us in this opening.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4p3/1B6/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black accepts.

And we'll get the queen out already to attack the f7-pawn.

This might confuse a lot of players.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Study 2 of the first chapter, we will take a look at alternatives for Black on move 6.

They don't have to protect the pawn on e4 with the bishop.

They can also protect it with the queen or even leave it hanging.

r1b1k2r/pp1nbppp/1qp1pn2/6B1/3PN2Q/PB3N2.text:
And finally, we'll get the dark-squared bishop out.

This puts more pressure on the knight on f6 and keeps our queen safe.

We are actually planning to castle queenside, anticipating Black's kingside castling.

We've already got a lot of pieces on the kingside and could start an attack soon.

r1b1k2r/pp1nbppp/1qp1pn2/8/3PN2Q/PB3N2/1.text: That's why Black has to resort to passive development here.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/8/3Pn2Q/1B3N2/PP.text:
Once Black takes the knight...

Simply recapture.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/8/3Pn2Q/1B6/PPP1.text:
This capture doesn't bother us at all.

We'll just take back.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/8/4Q3/1B3N2/PPPP.text:
They'll most likely develop like this.

One of the main plans is to bring the knight to f6.

Sure, Black can go for that.

We'll go for central expansion.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1pn2/8/3PN2Q/1B6/PPP.text:
Black castles.

And we'll prepare to do so as well.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1pn2/8/4N2Q/1B6/PPPP.text:
Black continues by supporting the knight.

Their idea is most likely to trade now. That gives us enough room to strike with d4.

Simply utilizing our usual ideas.

If 9...Nd5 you can play 10.Qg3.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/8/3P4/1B3N2/PPP1.text:
This is the standard retreating square, as we keep some potential for the queen while maintaining its safety.

We want to play Bd2 or e3 and castle queenside. 

c3 and Bc2 is a smart maneuver if necessary. We should have a solid middlegame.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/8/3P4/1B3Q2/PPP1.text:
Our queen has a safe square on f3.

From here, it is both safe and active.

The knight on e2 is doing a great job defending the center and we are ready to castle.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/8/3PQ3/1B3N2/PPP.text: And retreat to e2 once the queen is attacked.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/8/3PQ3/1B6/PPP1N.text: Even if the knight arrives on f6...

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/8/3P4/1B6/PPP1QPP.text:
Black castles...

And our knight gets activated on f3.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/8/3PQ3/1B6/PPP2PP.text: We'll still expand in the center and play a comfortable game.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/8/4Q3/1B6/PPPP1PP.text: Black could develop the bishop before jumping to f6, which shouldn't change our plans too much.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/2p1pn2/8/4N2Q/1B6/PPPP1.text:
One of the options is to support the f6-knight with the knight on d7.

Black wants a knight on the f6-square no matter what.

Since there haven't been any confrontations so far, we can simply continue with d4.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/8/8/1B6/PPPPQPPP/R.text:
Black goes ahead with their plan, ready to castle.

An upside to capturing the pawn on e4 is always...The fact that we can play d4!

This is something you should always look out for in the Hillbilly.

Next, we'll finish kingside development.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/1pp1p3/8/8/1P2Q3/1PPP1PPP.text: Black will probably defend with ...b6 here.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/1pp1p3/8/8/1P2QN2/1PPP1PP.text:
After which you can simply continue natural development.

Our rook is open, we will play d4 soon to expand in the center and castle.

A nice position for White, although equal.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/8/4n2Q/1B6/PPPP1.text:
Black trades.

And we'll recapture with the queen.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/8/4p2Q/1BN5/PPP.text:
The move 6...Nbd7 is only played 8% of the time, but has a concrete idea behind it.

We shouldn't let them play ...Nc5 and defend everything.

Another plan for Black is to let us capture the pawn in the center, trade, and then bring the d7-knight to f6.

We'll let them, as grabbing the pawn is still good here.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/2n5/4Q3/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
An alternative to ...Nf6 that you might encounter is ...Nc5.

Black might think it's the superior move because they are forking our queen and our bishop.

But our bishop wasn't that active to begin with since Black blocked its vision with ...e6.

And you will soon see why we are moving the queen to the e3-square.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/8/1n2Q3/PPPP1PPP.text:
So we can let them capture and trade off their only active piece.

We'll take back with the a-pawn, and suddenly the a7-pawn is under attack.

Black has to weaken their pawn structure to defend that.

This was the point of Qe3.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/8/4Q3/1B6/PPPP1PP.text:
As mentioned, Black's main idea is to get the knight to f6 now with tempo.

They want to get the dark-squared bishop out quickly and castle.

We'll move to e2.

Our queen is safest there and doesn't need to be roaming the board until we develop more pieces.

r1bqr1k1/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/8/3P4/1B3N2/PPP1Q.text:
Black lines up the rook with our queen, but there's the e6-pawn to block that.

So we can relax for now.

Castling is sufficient here.

Black might want to play ...e5 at some point, but can't right now.

It would be a big mistake as it would allow Ng5.

rnb1k2r/pp2bppp/1qp1pn2/8/4N2Q/PB3N2/1PP.text:
Which is why ...Bf6 is logical, defending.

Black doesn't have any useful discovered attacks here, so we don't have to move the queen.

We can focus on expanding in the center instead, which is our primary concern when Black's e4-pawn is removed.

Another benefit of playing d4 here is that we disable Black from playing ...e5 anytime soon.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qp1pn2/8/4p2Q/PBN2N2/1P.text:
So Black retreats to b6.

Premature play indeed, allowing us to develop with tempo like this.

And eventually grab the pawn in the center and equalize the material.

We are threatening to take on f6 now as well.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/8/1q2p2Q/1BN2N2/P.text:
So they slide to b4.

Let's continue chasing the queen.

And we'll do that with a3.

The queen now can't stay on the fourth rank anymore.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/8/3qp2Q/1BN5/PPPP.text:
We've already seen 6...Qd4 in the chapter on 4...g6.

It does protect the pawn and activate the queen but it's already a complication because the pawn is now pinned to the queen.

It's played 13% of the time.

We'll take advantage of that and develop with tempo, and Black now has to keep an eye on the e4-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1p3/8/4Q3/1B6/PPPP1PP.text:
Black castles.

And we'll play Nf3.

Black can't prevent d4 either way, so we don't have to rush with it.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/8/4N2Q/1B6/PPPP1.text:
Black can also choose to castle here, which is the other main idea of 6...Be7.

In this case, I suggest we develop the knight to e2.

We want to leave the f3-square free for the queen to escape to in case it is attacked.

From e2, the knight also supports d4, which is what we want to play.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/2p1p3/8/4n2Q/1B6/PPPP1PP.text:
The move that's played more than half the time is ...Nxe4.

Black wants to trade off our active knight from the center.

We'll recapture, of course.

Natural development to follow.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/8/4p2Q/1BN5/PPPP1.text:
The most common move is 6...Be7, played 67% of the time.

Black wants to set up some discovered attacks on our queen, while preparing to castle kingside.

We can just capture the pawn.

Nothing to worry about.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/7Q/4p3/1BN5/PPPP1.text:
The most logical move is to develop, defend the pawn and attack our queen at the same time.

As in the 4...g6 chapter, we will slide the queen to h4.

It's safe on that square and attacks the e4-pawn.

Black has got multiple ways of approaching the position here.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The Caro-Kann.

Let's play the Hillbilly.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2B1P3/8/PPPP1PP.text:
Black advances in the center.

We'll retreat and gambit the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4p3/1B6/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black captures...

And we'll attack with the queen as per usual.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/7Q/4p3/1B6/PPPP1PP.text:
Black doesn't challenge our queen but rather blocks their bishop with ...e6 and stops the attack that way.

This move is played almost 40% of the time, which equals to almost 70,000 games.

Since our queen hasn't been attacked, we will just develop and hit the pawn on e4 which Black often has trouble protecting.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Chapter 2, we will focus on Black covering the queen and bishop attack with ...e6 on move 4.

This move blocks our bishop but blocks the Black bishop at the same time and could turn out to be pretty committal.

Let's begin.

lessons.title: Early Sidelines and Bad Moves in the Hillbilly

rn1qkb1r/pp2p2p/2p2ppn/5b2/4Q3/1BN5/PPPP.text: Sure, it can get pushed around a bit...

rn1qkb1r/pp2p2p/2p2ppn/5b2/8/1BN5/PPPPQP.text:
But the e2-square is safe.

Now that we captured the central e4-pawn, we are aiming to play Nf3 and d4 to expand further.

Black has played the unnecessary ...Nh6 and now their pieces and pawns are weirdly placed on the kingside, creating weaknesses.

White is much better here.

rnbq1b1r/pp1kpQpp/2p2n2/8/4p3/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
Black has to move to d7.

Don't rush here as there is no checkmate. Your position is convincingly winning as it is.

The simple Nc3 suffices.

We don't have to hurry attacking the king now.

rnbq1b1r/ppk1pQpp/2p2n2/8/4p3/1BN5/PPPP1.text: Black will have to spend some moves freeing their pieces either way.

rnbq1b1r/ppk1pQpp/2p2n2/8/4p3/1BNP4/PPP2.text:
Meanwhile, we can open up our bishop and look to play Bf4+.

After that, we'll castle queenside and enjoy an amazing position.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3P4/1B6/PPP.text:
First, they play ...e6 to protect the center.

Anticipating this...

We'll strengthen our pawn chain.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/1BP5/PP2.text:
We can simply bring the knight to e2, and look to play Nd2-Nf3.

This structure with the knights on e2 and f3 is important, as we would have a hard time developing the b1-knight otherwise.

Apart from that, our bishop will now be stronger on c2 than on b3.

And we'll castle, of course.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/1BP5/PP3.text:
They can play ...c5 all they want.

Our pawns are strong together.

rnbqkb1r/pp1npppp/2p5/3pP3/8/1B6/PPPP1PP.text:
The smarter move out of the two is ...Nfd7.

Black retreats but attacks our pawn.

This forces us to play d4.

Black's idea is ...c5 to try and strike back.

rnbqkb1r/pp2p2p/2p2ppn/4Q3/4p3/1BN5/PPPP.text:
Black has to play ...f6 and make more holes in their position.

We'll just take in the center and keep our queen active.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p3pn/7Q/4p3/1BN5/PPPP1.text:
Black can play ...g6 now to attack our queen.

But why not play it a move earlier?

In this case, ...g6 is a mistake when the knight is on h6.

Because our queen can slide to the center and there is no ...Nf6 to block.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/4P3/1B6/PPPP1.text:
Instead of capturing, Black players choose ...Nf6 here 11% of the time.

They want to develop the knight as quickly as possible thinking they're simply adding an attacker to the pawn.

But they sometimes forget that we can simply push e5, save the pawn and attack the knight.

And this is the best move.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/7Q/4p3/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
Of course, ...Nf6 is an obvious blunder.

Let's just demonstrate how to approach this winning position.

We'll take on f7 with check, of course.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p4n/7Q/4p3/1B6/PPPP1PP.text:
They can try to protect the pawn with ...Nh6.

This is as ugly as it looks.

The knight is completely stranded on h6 and there is no need for Black to play like this.

We'll simply continue with Nc3, attacking the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/4n3/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
Jumping to the center only makes matters worse for Black.

Instead of attacking the knight, let's take away one of its escape squares.

And d4 is the best way to do that, also grabbing central space.

Now the knight doesn't actually have any escape squares. We are threatening to push f3 and win it.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3Pn3/1B6/PPP1.text:
But Ne2 neutralizes this threat.

Now we can push g3 in case of the ...Qh4+ check, so both f3 and g3 are on the cards.

On the queenside, we'll play c3 to solidify the pawn chain and play Nd2 once Black's knight has been either won or somehow saved.

And the only way to try and save it is push ...f6, which is just sad.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3Pn3/1B6/PPP2.text:
A witty attempt to fight against this is ...e6.

Black wants ...Qh4+ if we play f3.

And that would be winning for them, indeed.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The Caro-Kann.

We'll go for the Hillbilly.

In the video I covered the weird and bad moves 2...d6 and 2...e6. We get simple play and can often develop straightforwardly.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2B1P3/8/PPPP1PP.text:
2...d5 is still the most common move.

However, Black can choose not to capture on e4 once we retreat with the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4p3/1B6/PPPP1PPP/.text:
This is the main line we saw in the previous chapters.

However, Black can try to play a different move than ...g6 or ...e6 here.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/4P3/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
Black can try to neutralize our bishop further with ...e6.

This is designed for Black to play ...c5 soon and keep an eye on d5.

It's played only 8% of the time, though.

First, we'll protect our pawn.

Our idea is to play d4 if allowed and cover that c5-square.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/3pP3/1BN5/PPPP1P.text:
However, Black might anticipate that and play ...d4 themselves!

This line will give them space but we will have a lot of counterplay.

We'll retreat to e2.

It looks passive but our knight will rejoin the game later.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2p5/3pP3/1B1P4/PPP1N.text:
So I suggest d3 here.

It connects the pawn chain and we are preparing to push f4 to grab space on the kingside, followed by Nf3.

If Black goes for ...e5 to open up their bishop, that opens up our bishop on b3 as well and f4 is even more potent then.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2p5/3pP3/1B6/PPPPNPP.text:
As mentioned, ...d4 and ...c5 are the ideas to grab space.

We don't want to give Black too much room, however.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The final chapter of the Hillbilly will deal with the deviations Black can make on different moves.

We will cover deviations as soon as move 2, as well as deviations all the way to move 5.

Let's go.
